title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Branch is a Name; a Merge is a Node with Two Parents
Creating a branch does not copy files. It writes a ref. Merging either slides that ref (fast-forward) or writes a commit with two parents (a join).

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

git switch -c feat = write refs/heads/feat at current HEAD, point HEAD at it.
Fast-forward is legal iff the current tip is an ancestor of the other tip.
A three-way merge diffs base→ours and base→theirs and applies both to the base. The merge base is the unique best common ancestor (usually).
Conflict markers are unmerged index stages (1 base, 2 ours, 3 theirs) spilled into the working tree.
During a merge, --ours is HEAD. During a rebase, --ours is the upstream. That swap is the theory, not a bug.

 fast-forward          three-way merge

 A ← B ← C   main      A ← B ← C ← M   main
           ← D ← E           ↑     ↑
                             D ← E

title: Theory
text:
Why merge commits exist
They record that two lines of work met, and they keep both sides’ hashes stable. Rebase prefers a straight first-parent chain and pays with new hashes. Neither changes the fact that Git stores snapshots.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Merging with uncommitted work that overlaps the incoming tree.
Resolving markers but forgetting git add (merge stays open).
git merge --abort after the merge commit exists (too late).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Create/switch, merge types, three-way, conflicts, fast-forward, lab; then mergetool, ours/theirs, orphan, comparing branches, rerere.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
Branch to Create a Safe Working Area
After this page you can create, switch, list, and delete branches on Linux without touching main.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
A branch is a name
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git branch
git switch -c feat/ping-json
git branch
git switch -c creates feat/ping-json at current HEAD and points HEAD at it. git branch (no args) lists local names; * is where HEAD is.
git switch main
git switch feat/ping-json
git switch is the modern command. git checkout still works; this book uses switch for branches.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
section: Name them so later pages stay readable
text:
Name them so later pages stay readable
feat/…     a capability
fix/…      a bug
chore/…    tooling
Slashes are fine on Linux. The name is a file under .git/refs/heads/ (or a line in packed-refs). feat/ping-json is the path refs/heads/feat/ping-json.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
Work on the branch
git switch feat/ping-json
# edit, add, commit as in chapter 3
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate
main stays where you left it. Commits on feat/ping-json are extra nodes in the DAG.
 A ← B ← C                 main
           ↖
             D ← E         feat/ping-json   HEAD

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
List and see
git branch -v                 # last commit on each
git branch --show-current
git log --oneline main..HEAD  # commits on this branch that main does not have
A..B means reachable from B, not from A.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
Delete
git switch main
git branch -d feat/ping-json     # refuses if not merged
git branch -D feat/ping-json     # delete anyway
-d is the default you want. -D is when you meant to throw the line of work away.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
Rename
git branch -m feat/ping-json feat/ping
Renames the current branch if you omit the old name. After you publish a branch, renaming locally does not rename it on the remote; chapter 11.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
section: Stuck with a dirty working tree
text:
Stuck with a dirty working tree
Git refuses to switch if the switch would overwrite uncommitted edits. Commit, stash (chapter 12), or restore first.
git status

title: Merge Types
text:
Merge Types: Fast-Forward, Recursive, and Octopus
After this page you can name the three merge shapes Git actually writes.

title: Merge Types
text:
Fast-forward
main is an ancestor of feat/ping-json. Merging can just slide main forward. No new commit.
A ← B ← C                 main
          ← D ← E         feat/ping-json

# after git switch main && git merge feat/ping-json

A ← B ← C ← D ← E         main, feat/ping-json
git switch main
git merge feat/ping-json
git log shows a straight line. git merge --no-ff forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible (Git Flow likes that; trunk-based usually does not).

title: Merge Types
text:
Recursive (two parents)
The branches diverged. Git writes a merge commit with two parents.
A ← B ← C ← M             main
     ↑      ↑
     D ← E                feat/ping-json
The default strategy for two heads is ort (the current “recursive” replacement). You rarely pass -s. Git finds a merge base (common ancestor), diffs both sides against it, and applies both diffs to the base.
git switch main
git merge feat/ping-json -m "merge feat/ping-json"
git log --oneline --graph --decorate

title: Merge Types
text:
Octopus (three or more parents)
git merge topic-a topic-b topic-c
One merge commit with several parents. Git only does this when there are no overlapping conflicts. If two topics touch the same hunk, octopus refuses; merge them pairwise instead. You will almost never need octopus on desk-api. Know the name so git log --graph with a commit that has three parents is not a mystery.
 A ← B ← C ← M          main     M has three parents
      ↑  ↑   ↑
      D  E   F          three topic tips

title: Merge Types
text:
See the parents
git cat-file -p HEAD
git rev-parse HEAD^1 HEAD^2
HEAD^1 is the first parent (the branch you had checked out). HEAD^2 is what you merged in.

title: Merge Types
text:
Abort
git merge --abort
Returns the three trees to the pre-merge state while a merge is in progress (MERGE_HEAD exists). After the merge commit exists, abort is too late; git reset (chapter 7) or git revert -m 1 (chapter 10).

title: Three-Way Merge
text:
Three-Way Merge Explained
After this page you can draw the three inputs Git uses when two branches diverged.

title: Three-Way Merge
text:
The three trees
Call them:



Name
What




Base
Merge base: latest common ancestor of both tips


Ours
The branch you have checked out (HEAD)


Theirs
The branch you named in git merge



Git diffs base→ours and base→theirs, then applies both diffs to the base. That is a three-way merge. A two-way merge (ours vs theirs only) cannot tell “we both added the same line” from “they added a line we never had.”
          C  base     (merge-base main feat)
         / \
        /   \
      G     E         ours = main, theirs = feat
        \   /
         \ /
          M  result   two-parent merge commit

title: Three-Way Merge
text:
See the base
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git merge-base main feat/ping-json
git log --oneline --graph main feat/ping-json
merge-base prints one hash. git log --graph should make that node obvious.

title: Three-Way Merge
section: Stages in the index during a conflict
text:
Stages in the index during a conflict
When both sides changed the same hunk, Git records three stages for that path in the index:



Stage
Content




1
base


2
ours


3
theirs



git ls-files -u
git checkout --ours path / --theirs path copies stage 2 or 3 into the working tree. You still git add after you edit. The next page is the full conflict loop.

title: Three-Way Merge
section: Why this matters for a forge
text:
Why this matters for a forge
A pull request / merge request is this same three-way merge, run on the server when you click Merge. The conflict you see in the UI is stages 2 and 3 plus markers. Learning it locally means the UI is not a new theory.

title: Three-Way Merge
text:
zdiff3 markers
With merge.conflictstyle zdiff3 (chapter 2) a conflicted file shows the common ancestor as well as ours and theirs. That extra block is the base. Read it before you delete markers.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
Merge Conflicts: In Git and in Teams
After this page you can finish a conflicted merge on Linux and leave a clean main.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
What a conflict is
Both branches changed the same region of a file (or one side changed a file the other deleted). Git writes conflict markers into the working tree and leaves the merge unfinished.
<<<<<<< HEAD
return "ok"
=======
return {"status": "ok"}
>>>>>>> feat/ping-json
With zdiff3 you also get an ancestor block (|||||||).

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
The loop
git switch main
git merge feat/ping-json
# Git stops and prints "fix conflicts and then commit"

git status
# both modified: src/ping.py
Edit the file in nvim. Remove every <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> (and ||||||| if present). Leave the code you want.
git add src/ping.py
git status          # "all conflicts fixed"
git commit          # default message is "Merge branch 'feat/ping-json'"
Git opens core.editor for the merge message if you omit -m. A conventional subject is optional here; merge commits are often left as Git’s default so git log --first-parent stays readable.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
Abort vs continue
git merge --abort     # give up; back to pre-merge
After git add, there is no --continue for merge; git commit finishes it. Rebase does use --continue (chapter 9).

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
Binary files and deletes
git status will say deleted by them or added by us. Pick a side:
git restore --ours --worktree --staged path
git restore --theirs --worktree --staged path
git rm path
Then git add / git commit as usual.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
Teams
A conflict is a data problem (two diffs) plus a people problem (whose behavior should win). On a forge, the same markers appear in the pull-request UI. Resolve on your laptop, commit, push. Do not resolve only in the UI if you cannot run the tests; Linux is where desk-api actually runs.
rerere (chapter 2) records how you resolved a hunk and reapplies it if the same conflict comes back. Leave it enabled.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
After the merge
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git branch -d feat/ping-json
-d succeeds once the work is reachable from main.

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
Creating a Fast-Forward Merge for a Clean History
After this page you can keep main a straight line when the feature branch is ahead of it.

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
When a fast-forward is possible
main has not moved since you branched. Every commit on the feature is a descendant of main.
 before --ff-only                   after --ff-only

 A ← B ← C          main            A ← B ← C ← D ← E   main
           ← D ← E  feat                        feat
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git merge --ff-only feat/ping-json
--ff-only fails if Git would need a merge commit. That is the setting you already put in pull.ff only for pulls. Use it on purpose for local merges when you want a linear main.

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
If it fails
Someone committed to main while you worked. Options:

Merge anyway (git merge feat/ping-json) → merge commit, history shows the join.
Rebase the feature onto main (chapter 9), then --ff-only.
git merge --no-ff feat/ping-json → always a merge commit (Git Flow release style).

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
See it
git log --oneline --graph --decorate
A fast-forward looks like a single chain. A merge commit is a join with two parents.

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
first-parent
git log --first-parent --oneline
Walks only ^1. After --no-ff merges, this is “what landed on main.” After a fast-forward, it is the same as a normal log. Chapter 15 picks a branching strategy; this page is the mechanism that strategy will call.

EOF

Branch B — string change on main

EOF
git add src/ping.py
git commit -m "feat(ping): shout the status"
main and feat/ping-json have diverged.
 A ← B ← C ← shout     main          ping.py returns "OK"
           ↖
             dict      feat/ping-json  ping.py returns {"status": "ok"}

Merge and conflict

git status
cat src/ping.py
You should see markers. Open the file in nvim (or your editor) and make it:

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Rebase Copies Commits; It Does Not Slide Them
A rebase walks a range of commits, takes each patch against its parent, and applies it onto a new base. Each successful apply writes a new commit (new hash, usually same author, you as committer).

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Original commits remain in the object store until GC; the branch name moves to the copied tip.
Conflicts happen once per copied commit, not once at a join.
Interactive rebase is the same machine plus a todo list (pick, squash, fixup, reword, edit, drop).
pull --rebase = fetch + rebase local-only commits onto @{u}.
--onto is “take this range and replay it on that commit,” the general form of rebase.

 before                         after git rebase main

 A ← B ← C ← G     main         A ← B ← C ← G          main
      ↑                                     ↖
      D ← E        feat                       D' ← E'  feat

title: Theory
text:
Why teams fight about it
Merge preserves hashes and adds a node. Rebase rewrites hashes and can keep main linear. Unpublished feature branches are the safe audience. Published main is not.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Rebasing commits other people have based work on (force-push incident).
--ours/--theirs confusion vs merge.
Empty commits after rebase (--skip vs keep).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Why, interactive, conflicts, pull –rebase, vs merge, lab; then --onto, autosquash, --exec, --update-refs.

title: Why Rebase
text:
Why Rebase? Clean History vs Merge Commits
After this page you can say what rebase copies, and why the hashes change.

title: Why Rebase
section: Replay commits on a new parent
text:
Replay commits on a new parent
You branched from main at C. main moved to G. Rebase copies your commits D and E as D' and E' with parent G:
A ← B ← C ← G                main
          ← D ← E            feat/ping-json

# git switch feat/ping-json && git rebase main

A ← B ← C ← G                main
              ← D' ← E'      feat/ping-json
D' has a new hash. The patch is similar; the parent is G. Git then fast-forwards or you --ff-only merge into main.
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch feat/ping-json
git rebase main

title: Why Rebase
text:
What you gain

main can stay a single chain (fast-forward).
Reviewers read your commits on top of current main, not an old base.
git log --first-parent on main after --ff-only is your feature commits, not a merge node.

title: Why Rebase
text:
What you pay

New hashes. Anyone who fetched D and E now has stale names.
Conflicts are replayed per copied commit, not once in a merge commit.

Rebase unpublished work (your feature branch). Merge published history you share (main that others pulled). Chapter 11 is force-push if you already pushed the old D and E.

title: Why Rebase
section: rebase vs merge in one line
text:
rebase vs merge in one line
Merge adds a join. Rebase copies a chain onto a new base. Both produce a tree that contains both sides of the work. The graph looks different. The next pages are interactive rebase, conflicts, pull --rebase, and when to pick which.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Interactive Rebase: Squash, Reorder, Fixup, Polish
After this page you can rewrite a short chain of local commits on Linux without a GUI.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Open the todo list
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch feat/ping-json
git rebase -i HEAD~3
Git writes a file and opens core.editor (nvim in this book). Each line is a commit, oldest first:
pick a1b2c3d feat(ping): return a dict
pick d4e5f6a docs: mention JSON
pick 98ab765 fix typo
You edit the verbs, save, quit. Git replays from the top.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Verbs you will use







Verb
Effect




pick
Keep this commit


reword
Keep, edit the message


edit
Stop here so you can amend


squash
Fold into the previous commit; editor for a combined message


fixup
Fold into the previous commit; keep the previous message


drop
Omit this commit



Reorder lines to reorder commits. Delete a line to drop (same as drop).

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Linux without the editor (labs)
For a scripted squash of everything after the first of the last three:
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR="sed -i '2,\$s/^pick /fixup /'" git rebase -i HEAD~3
sed -i on GNU sed (Linux) edits in place. This is for labs and hooks. Day to day, use nvim.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Stop and amend (edit)
Git stops at that commit. You git add / git commit --amend, then:
git rebase --continue

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Abort
git rebase --abort
Back to the pre-rebase branch tip. Safe while the rebase is in progress.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Range
git rebase -i main rebases each commit reachable from HEAD but not from main. That is the usual “update my feature onto main” todo list.
Do this on a feature branch. Interactive rebase of shared main rewrites hashes everyone already has.

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
Rebase Conflicts: How They Differ from Merge Conflicts
After this page you can finish a conflicted rebase one commit at a time.

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
One commit at a time
A merge conflict happens once, at the join. A rebase conflict happens each time a copied commit does not apply onto the new parent.
 merge: one fight at M

 A ← B ← C ← M
      ↑      ↑
      D ← E

 rebase: a fight at D', then maybe again at E'

 A ← B ← C ← G ← D'  ←  E'
                 ▲ stop    ▲ stop
Markers look the same (<<<<<<<). git status during a rebase says rebase in progress and names the commit being applied.
git rebase main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/ping.py
git status

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
The loop

Edit files, remove markers.
git add the resolved paths.
git rebase --continue (not git commit, unless Git asks you to).
Repeat until Git prints Successfully rebased.

nvim src/ping.py
git add src/ping.py
git rebase --continue
If the commit becomes empty (your patch is already in the new base):
git rebase --skip
Give up:
git rebase --abort

title: Rebase Conflicts
section: Ours / theirs are swapped from merge
text:
Ours / theirs are swapped from merge
During merge, --ours is the branch you had checked out (main). During rebase, you checked out the feature and Git replays onto main: --ours is the upstream (the new base), --theirs is the commit being replayed.
That swap surprises everyone once. Prefer reading the markers over --ours until it is boring.

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
rerere
With rerere.enabled (chapter 2), Git records the resolution. A later rebase that hits the same hunk applies it again. On a long-lived feature branch that rebases onto main daily, this is the difference between pain and a two-second continue.

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
After success
git log --oneline --graph --decorate main feat/ping-json
A straight line from main through your copied commits. Then git switch main && git merge --ff-only feat/ping-json.

title: Pull with Rebase
text:
Pull with Rebase When Your Branch Is Out of Date
After this page you can update a local branch from a remote without a merge commit from git pull.

title: Pull with Rebase
text:
pull is fetch plus integrate
git pull
means git fetch then, by default, a merge of @{u} (the upstream) into HEAD. If both you and the remote moved, you get a merge commit that only exists because you pulled.
 after fetch, both moved

 origin/main   A ← B ← C ← G
 local main    A ← B ← C ← D ← E

 git pull              (merge)     A ← B ← C ← G ← M
                                         D ← E ↗

 git pull --rebase                 A ← B ← C ← G ← D' ← E'
Chapter 2 set:
git config --global pull.ff only
Then git pull fails instead of merging. You choose:
git pull --rebase
# or
git fetch
git rebase @{u}
--rebase copies your local-only commits onto the updated upstream, then fast-forwards your branch name.

title: Pull with Rebase
section: When this is the right shape
text:
When this is the right shape
You committed two fixes on main locally. Someone else pushed to origin/main. git pull --rebase replays your two fixes on top of theirs. History stays linear. Conflicts are per commit (previous page).

title: Pull with Rebase
text:
When to merge instead
You want a merge commit that records “I integrated upstream at this point.” Feature branches that you share, or main policies that require merge commits, use git pull --no-rebase or an explicit git merge.

title: Pull with Rebase
section: Set it for this branch only
text:
Set it for this branch only
git config pull.rebase true          # this repo
git config --global pull.rebase true # every repo (overrides pull.ff only)
This book leaves pull.ff only as the global default so a surprise pull fails closed. Type --rebase when you mean it, until the habit is there.

title: Pull with Rebase
text:
After a rebase pull
git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -12
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by N commits means you still need git push. If you had already pushed the old hashes, you need a force-with-lease (chapter 11).

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
The Debate: Rebase vs Merge
After this page you can pick a default for desk-api and know what you are giving up.

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
Same trees, different graphs
Both operations can produce a working tree that contains both sides of the work. Merge records a join. Rebase copies a chain.
 start                         after merge

 A ← B ← C ← G   main          A ← B ← C ← G ← M   main
      ↑                             ↑          ↑
      D ← E      feat               D ← E      feat

 start                         after rebase feat onto main

 A ← B ← C ← G   main          A ← B ← C ← G          main
      ↑                                      ↖
      D ← E      feat                          D' ← E'  feat




Merge
Rebase




Hashes of your old commits
Unchanged
New


Extra commit
Often a merge commit
None if you fast-forward after


Conflicts
Once, at the join
Once per copied commit


Safe on published main
Yes
Usually no


Safe on your unpushed feature
Yes
Yes, and often cleaner

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
A default that scales

Feature branch you own: rebase onto main, then fast-forward main (or open a pull request that the forge squash-merges).
main / shared long-lived branch: merge or fast-forward only. Do not rebase commits other people have.
Hotfix already on main: revert (chapter 10), do not rebase main.

Forges add a third option: squash merge (many commits become one on main). That is a server-side rewrite. Chapter 15 and chapter 31. Locally, rebase is how you squash before you push.

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
rerere, tests, Linux
Run the test command you actually have after every --continue. On Linux that is whatever desk-api uses (python -m pytest, a shell script, make test). Rebase does not run tests for you.

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
You can mix
Rebase the feature. Merge into main with --no-ff if the team wants a join node for git log --first-parent. That is Git Flow’s “feature into develop” shape. Trunk-based skips the join and fast-forwards.
There is no global winner. There is a default per branch class. Write it down in the repo (chapter 15). The hands-on page next squashes a messy feature on Linux.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Cherry-Pick and Revert are Patches with New Hashes
Both operations take a diff (commit vs its parent, or the inverse) and apply it to HEAD, writing a new commit. They do not move the original node.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Cherry-pick(C) ≈ apply diff(parent(C), C) onto HEAD.
Revert(C) ≈ apply diff(C, parent(C)) onto HEAD (the inverse patch).
The original commit remains reachable if any name still points at it.
Revert of a merge needs -m to choose which parent is the mainline; Git then considers those changes “already merged” for future merges.
-x records cherry picked from in the message; it does not link objects.

 cherry-pick D onto main          revert C on main

 feat  A ← B ← C ← D ← E          A ← B ← C ← R
 main  A ← B ← C                  R undoes C; C stays
 after A ← B ← C ← D'

title: Theory
text:
Why not reset on production
Reset moves a name backward. Clones that already have the old tip cannot fast-forward. Revert lets them fast-forward to a commit that cancels the bad one. That is the distributed-model consequence, not etiquette.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Cherry-picking a merge without -m.
Reverting a merge then trying to merge the same feature again (Git thinks it is in).
Secrets: revert does not purge blobs from history.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Cherry-pick, hotfixes, revert, emergencies; then ranges/-x, empty picks.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Cherry-Pick: Moving Commits Surgically
After this page you can copy one commit onto another branch without merging the whole feature.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Copy the patch, new hash
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git cherry-pick <hash>
Git takes the diff of that commit against its parent, applies it onto HEAD, and writes a new commit. The new object has a new hash. Author is preserved; you are the committer.
 feat    A ← B ← C ← D ← E          pick D only
 main    A ← B ← C

 after   A ← B ← C ← D'             main   (D' ≈ patch of D, new hash)
 feat    A ← B ← C ← D ← E          unchanged
git log -1 --format=fuller

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Several commits
git cherry-pick abc123 def456
git cherry-pick main~3..feat/ping-json
A range A..B is commits reachable from B excluding A. Oldest is applied first.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Conflicts
Same markers as merge. Then:
git add src/ping.py
git cherry-pick --continue
git cherry-pick --abort
git cherry-pick --skip
Same loop as rebase, one commit at a time.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Empty pick
If main already contains the change, Git says the pick is empty. --skip or --allow-empty.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
What cherry-pick is for

A hotfix that lives on a release branch and also needs to be on main
A commit that landed on the wrong branch
Backporting a fix to an older release/* line

What it is a poor fit for: dragging a whole feature. Merge or rebase the branch instead so you get the whole chain and a honest graph.
Next page: hotfixes and backports as a desk scenario.

title: Hotfixes and Backports
text:
Deploying Hotfixes Without Merging Features
After this page you can land a one-commit fix on main and on a release branch without dragging unreleased work.

title: Hotfixes and Backports
text:
The situation
feat/big-refactor is half done. Production (main or release/1.x) needs a one-line fix that you already committed on the feature branch.
Merging the feature would ship unfinished work. Cherry-pick the fix commit only.
 feat/big-refactor   A ← B ← fix ← D ← E     (D,E not ready)
 main                A ← B

 cherry-pick fix     A ← B ← fix'            main
                     A ← B ← fix ← D ← E     feat  (untouched)
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git log feat/big-refactor --oneline -5
# copy the hash of the fix

git switch main
git cherry-pick <hash>

title: Hotfixes and Backports
text:
Release branch
git switch -c release/1.2 main   # or an existing release line
git cherry-pick <hash>
Now both lines have the fix, as two commits with different hashes and the same author.

title: Hotfixes and Backports
text:
Backport the other direction
The fix landed on main first. An older release still needs it:
git switch release/1.1
git cherry-pick <hash-on-main>
If the older tree cannot apply the patch (the surrounding code moved), resolve like a rebase conflict or rewrite the fix by hand and commit normally. Cherry-pick is a tool, not a guarantee.

title: Hotfixes and Backports
Hotfixes and Backports
text:
After the pick
Run whatever desk-api uses to check itself on Linux (python -c 'from src.ping import ping; print(ping())' is enough for the toy module). Then merge or push according to chapter 11. Do not merge feat/big-refactor until that feature is done.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
git revert and Unmerging Changes
After this page you can undo a published commit by adding a new commit, including a merge.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Revert writes history forward
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git revert HEAD --no-edit
git log --oneline -3
The bad commit is still in the graph. A new commit applies the inverse patch. Shared clones can fast-forward. This is the safe undo on main.
 reset --hard HEAD~1     (local only)     A ← B            main
                                          C still in reflog

 revert HEAD             (shared)         A ← B ← C ← R    main
                                          R undoes C; C remains
--no-edit keeps Git’s default message (Revert "…"). Edit with git revert HEAD if you need a fix: subject.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Several commits
git revert --no-edit HEAD~2..HEAD
Reverts newest first (the range is exclusive on the left). Conflicts: git add and git revert --continue, or git revert --abort.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Revert a merge commit
A merge has two parents. Git needs to know which parent is “the mainline” to diff against:
git revert -m 1 <merge-hash>
-m 1 means “keep first parent’s tree; undo what the merged branch brought in.” -m 2 is the other parent (almost never what you want on main).
After reverting a merge, Git considers that feature’s commits already merged. Cherry-picking them back later can no-op. To re-land the feature, revert the revert, or rebase the feature into new hashes.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Revert vs reset vs restore








Goal
Command
History




Throw away uncommitted edits
git restore
Unchanged


Replace last unpublished commit
git commit --amend / reset
Rewritten


Undo a published commit
git revert
New commit



git reset --hard on shared main is a force-push incident. Revert instead.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Un-merge without -m
If the merge was never pushed and is HEAD:
git reset --hard HEAD~1
That moves main to first parent and drops the merge commit from the branch name. Only on a lab clone or an unpublished branch. Chapter 7 is reset in full. The merge commit stays in the reflog (chapter 17) until it expires.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
text:
Real Production Emergency Scenarios
After this page you have a short playbook for “production is wrong and Git is how we talk about it.”
Assume Linux, ~/desk/desk-api, and a main that is already on a remote. You are in a terminal, not a GUI.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 1. Bad commit is HEAD on main, already pulled by others
text:
1. Bad commit is HEAD on main, already pulled by others
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git revert HEAD --no-edit
# run tests
git push

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 2. Bad commit is in the middle of main
text:
2. Bad commit is in the middle of main
git log --oneline -20
git revert --no-edit <hash>
# tests
git push
If several commits are one logical change, revert the range newest-first, or revert the merge with -m 1.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 3. Fix exists on a feature branch, production cannot wait
text:
3. Fix exists on a feature branch, production cannot wait
git log feat/whatever --oneline
git switch main
git cherry-pick -x <fix-hash>
# tests
git push
Leave the feature branch as-is. The pick is a new hash on main.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
text:
4. You committed a secret
git revert does not remove the secret from history; it only removes it from HEAD. Anyone who fetched still has the blob. Rotate the secret at the provider. History cleanup is chapter 20 (git filter-repo). For the next five minutes: revert or a follow-up commit that deletes the file, rotate, tell the team.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 5. Merge to main was wrong, merge commit is HEAD, not pushed
text:
5. Merge to main was wrong, merge commit is HEAD, not pushed
git reset --hard HEAD~1
If it was pushed, revert with -m 1 instead.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 6. You are not sure what main is
text:
6. You are not sure what main is
git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -15
git reflog -10
Status, graph, reflog. Then pick revert (shared) or reset (local only).
Write the team a one-line message: hash reverted, why, who is rotating secrets if any. Git is the record; the pager is the people.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Remote is Another Repository Plus a Nickname
origin is not special to Git. It is a default name for a URL. Fetch copies objects and updates remote-tracking refs. Push asks the other repository to move a name it owns.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

git fetch does not move your main. It updates refs/remotes/origin/main.
git pull = fetch + merge or rebase of @{u} into HEAD.
Non-fast-forward push is rejected because it would drop commits the remote still names.
--force-with-lease succeeds only if the remote ref still matches what you last fetched.
Several remotes means several photographs of the same DAG, not several Git identities.

  laptop                         origin (bare or forge)
  refs/heads/main                refs/heads/main
  refs/remotes/origin/main  ◄──  (fetch updates this)
         │ push ──────────────────►  (moves theirs if fast-forward)

title: Theory
section: Why PRs are not Git objects
text:
Why PRs are not Git objects
A pull request is a forge row: “please integrate this ref into that ref,” plus comments and checks. The Git underneath is still fetch + merge/rebase/squash on the server.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

git pull on a dirty tree.
Force-push of main.
Two remotes with the same objects but different main (divergent policy).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Fetch/pull/push, extra remotes, force-with-lease, PRs, two-clone lab; then upstream, refspecs, bundle, prune, fork vs clone.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Remote Mechanics: Fetch, Pull, Push
After this page you can talk to another Git repository on Linux without confusing fetch with pull.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
section: A remote is a named URL
text:
A remote is a named URL
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git remote add origin git@host:ada/desk-api.git
git remote -v
origin is a convention. The URL is SSH (chapter 2) or https://. For labs on one machine, a bare repo on disk is a valid remote:
 ~/desk/desk-api                         origin
 working tree + .git                     (bare) objects + refs
      │  git fetch    origin/main ──►    refs/heads/main
      │  git push     main ──────────►   refs/heads/main
      ▼
 refs/heads/main          refs/remotes/origin/main
git init --bare ~/desk/desk-api.git
git remote add origin ~/desk/desk-api.git
file:// and a path both work on Linux. Bare means no working tree — the shape a forge stores.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Fetch
git fetch origin
git fetch --all
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
Fetch downloads objects and updates remote-tracking names (origin/main). It does not move your main. Safe to run any time.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Push
git push -u origin main
-u sets upstream so later git push and git pull know the default. After that:
git push
git status
# Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'
Push refuses if the remote has commits you do not. Fetch, integrate, push again.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Pull
git pull
Fetch plus integrate @{u} into HEAD. With pull.ff only (chapter 2), it fast-forwards or fails. git pull --rebase copies your local commits onto the updated upstream (chapter 9).
Prefer git fetch then look at git log --oneline main..origin/main before you integrate.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Tracking
git branch -vv
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name '@{u}'
@{u} is the upstream of the current branch. git push -u is how it gets set.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Delete a remote branch
git push origin --delete feat/ping-json
Local delete is still git branch -d. The two are independent.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Understanding Multiple Remotes
After this page you can push the same desk-api history to two places.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Extra remotes are normal
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git remote add origin git@forgejo.home:ada/desk-api.git
git remote add github git@github.com:ada/desk-api.git
git remote -v
Fetch both:
git fetch --all
git branch -r
origin/main and github/main are separate photographs.
                    git push origin
                 ┌──────────────────►  Forgejo
 laptop desk-api ┤
                 └──────────────────►  GitHub
                    git push github

 refs/remotes/origin/main
 refs/remotes/github/main

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Push to both
git push origin main
git push github main
A convenience:
git remote add all git@forgejo.home:ada/desk-api.git
git remote set-url --add --push all git@forgejo.home:ada/desk-api.git
git remote set-url --add --push all git@github.com:ada/desk-api.git
git push all main
One git push all updates both push URLs. Fetch still uses the first URL of that remote unless you add more fetch URLs. Many people just type two pushes.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Independence preview
Chapter 22 is lock-in. The Git-level move is this page: the objects live in every clone. Two remotes means a forge outage does not strand desk-api. Issues and CI still live on each forge; Git history does not.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Rename and remove
git remote rename origin forgejo
git remote remove github
Removing a remote deletes remote-tracking refs for it. Local branches stay.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
origin on a USB disk
git init --bare /media/ada/stick/desk-api.git
git remote add stick /media/ada/stick/desk-api.git
git push -u stick main
Linux mounts the stick; Git sees a path. Same protocol family as ~/desk/desk-api.git.

title: Force Push
text:
Force Push Dangers
After this page you can update a remote after a rebase without clobbering someone else’s commits.

title: Force Push
text:
Why push refuses
You rebased feat/ping-json. Local hashes are new. The remote still has the old chain. A plain git push is a non-fast-forward and Git rejects it.
 origin/feat    A ← B ← C ← D ← E
 local feat     A ← B ← C ← G ← D' ← E'     (rebased onto new main)

 plain push     rejected (not a fast-forward)
 --force-with-lease
   if origin still at E  →  origin becomes E'
   if teammate added F   →  lease fails, fetch first

title: Force Push
text:
--force-with-lease
git push --force-with-lease origin feat/ping-json
Git checks that the remote ref still points at what you last fetched. If a teammate pushed in the meantime, the lease fails and you fetch again. That is the default force this book uses.

title: Force Push
text:
--force
git push --force origin feat/ping-json
Overwrites the remote ref even if it moved. Use on a branch only you own, and only when you meant to throw away the remote’s extra commits. Never a habit on main.

title: Force Push
text:
main
Do not force-push main on a shared remote. Revert instead (chapter 10). Forges often deny force on the default branch (chapter 31).

title: Force Push
section: Recover if you force-pushed by mistake
text:
Recover if you force-pushed by mistake
The old commits may still be on your laptop (git reflog) or another clone. Push them back:
git reflog
git push --force-with-lease origin <old-hash>:main   # only if you own this recovery
That is an emergency. Coordinate on chat first.

title: Force Push
text:
Lease plus fetch
Always:
git fetch origin
git log --oneline --graph --decorate HEAD origin/feat/ping-json
git push --force-with-lease
Look at the graph. Then push.

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Pull Requests, Code Review, and Handling Conflicts in Teams
After this page you can describe a pull request as Git operations plus a forge UI.

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
section: Git has no pull request object
text:
Git has no pull request object
A pull request (GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo, Bitbucket) or merge request (GitLab) is:

A branch you pushed (feat/ping-json)
A request that another branch (main) integrate it
Discussion, checks, and a button that runs merge, squash merge, or rebase merge on the server

Gerrit uses Change-Ids (chapter 27). SourceHut uses mailing lists (chapter 28). The Git underneath is still fetch + merge or rebase.
 origin/main     A ← B ← C
 origin/feat     A ← B ← C ← D ← E     ← you pushed this

 forge PR        "merge feat into main"
                 = merge, squash, or rebase on the server

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Local shape
git switch -c feat/ping-json
# commits
git push -u origin feat/ping-json
On the forge: open a PR from feat/ping-json into main. Reviewers fetch that branch:
git fetch origin feat/ping-json
git log --oneline main..origin/feat/ping-json
git switch -c review-ping origin/feat/ping-json

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Conflicts in a PR
The server’s merge is the same three-way merge as chapter 8. Resolve on Linux in your clone:
git fetch origin
git switch feat/ping-json
git rebase origin/main          # or: git merge origin/main
# fix, add, rebase --continue
git push --force-with-lease
The PR updates because the branch name moved.

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Review comments
Comments live on the forge. They are not Git objects. Closing a PR without merging leaves the branch on the remote until you delete it. Merging may delete the branch if the forge is set to.

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:

Your clone
If ~/desk/desk-api already has history:

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Stash is Commits; a Tag is a Name Meant to Stay Put
git stash writes commit objects (index state + working-tree state) and points refs/stash at them. A lightweight tag is a ref. An annotated tag is an object (message, tagger, date) that then points at a commit.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Stash does not change HEAD’s commit; it makes the working tree match HEAD (plus options for untracked).
stash@{n} is reflog syntax on refs/stash.
Tags are not pushed by default (git push origin v1.0.0).
git clean deletes untracked files Git never hashed; there is no Git undo.
git describe finds the nearest reachable annotated tag and counts commits after it.

  stash push                     annotated tag

  HEAD C  (unchanged)            refs/tags/v0.1.0 → tag object → commit C
  WD    clean
  refs/stash → W  (WIP commit)
                parent C

title: Theory
text:
Why stash vs a branch
A branch is a name you can push and PR. A stash is local, easy to drop, easy to lose in stash clear. If the WIP will survive the afternoon, switch -c wip/… and commit.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

stash pop with conflicts (entry may still drop).
Moving a published tag (-f) while others have already fetched it.
git clean -f -x deleting ignored .env.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter

title: Stash
text:
Stash Mechanics, Including Patch Stashes
After this page you can park uncommitted work, switch branches, and bring the work back.

title: Stash
section: A stash is a commit Git keeps on the side
text:
A stash is a commit Git keeps on the side
cd ~/desk/desk-api
echo "wip" >> README.md
git stash push -m "wip readme"
git status
git stash list
Working tree is clean. stash@{0} holds the diff. Switch branches, then:
 before stash                 after stash push

 working  dirty README        working  clean
 index    clean               index    clean
 HEAD     C                   HEAD     C
                              stash@{0}  ──► a pair of commits
                                           (index + working tree)
git stash pop
# or
git stash apply
pop applies and drops. apply applies and keeps the stash entry.

title: Stash
text:
Include untracked
git stash push -u -m "wip plus new files"
Without -u, untracked files stay in the way and can block a switch.

title: Stash
text:
Patch stash (-p)
git stash push -p -m "only the ping hunk"
Git offers hunks, same as git add -p. Stash the ones that are in the way; leave the rest in the working tree.

title: Stash
Stash
text:
Conflicts on apply
Markers appear. Add and continue as a normal working-tree conflict. The stash entry remains if you used apply; pop may still drop — prefer apply when you are unsure.

title: Stash
text:
Stash vs commit
A commit on a throwaway branch is easier to push and to recover. Stash is for “I must switch in the next ten seconds.” If the WIP will last, git switch -c wip/… and commit.

title: Tags
text:
Tags: Lightweight vs Annotated
After this page you can mark a commit as a release and push that name.

title: Tags
text:
Two kinds
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git tag v0.1.0                    # lightweight: a ref file
git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "desk-api 0.1.0"   # annotated: a tag object
Lightweight is a name pointing at a commit (like a branch that you do not move).
Annotated is a real object: message, tagger, date, optional signature (chapter 20). Releases should be annotated.
 lightweight                         annotated

 refs/tags/v0.1.0 ──► commit C       refs/tags/v0.1.0 ──► tag object
                                                              │
                                                              ▼
                                                         commit C
                                         tag object has message, tagger, date
If v0.1.0 already exists, Git refuses. git tag -f overwrites locally; moving a published tag surprises clones. Prefer v0.1.1.

title: Tags
text:
List and show
git tag
git tag -l 'v0.1.*'
git show v0.1.0

title: Tags
text:
Push
Tags are not pushed by default.
git push origin v0.1.0
git push origin --tags
--tags pushes all local tags. Prefer naming one tag for a release.

title: Tags
text:
Checkout
git switch --detach v0.1.0
Detached HEAD (chapter 1). Build or inspect, then git switch main. To develop from a tag: git switch -c hotfix/0.1.1 v0.1.0.

title: Tags
text:
Delete
git tag -d v0.1.0
git push origin --delete v0.1.0
Forges may still show a release page; that is forge metadata, not the Git tag.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Cleanup Commands
After this page you can delete merged branches, drop stashes, and remove untracked files on purpose.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Merged branches
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git branch --merged
git branch -d feat/readme-note
--merged lists names whose tips are reachable from HEAD. -d refuses otherwise; -D deletes anyway.
Remote leftovers:
git fetch --prune
git branch -r
--prune deletes remote-tracking names that the remote no longer has.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Stashes
git stash list
git stash drop stash@{0}
git stash clear          # every stash
clear is permanent for the stash reflog’s practical purposes. Apply first if you need the diff.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Untracked files: git clean
git clean -n             # dry run
git clean -n -d          # include untracked directories
git clean -f -d          # delete
-n is mandatory the first time you run it on a tree you care about. -f is required (Git refuses to delete without it). -x also removes ignored files (build artifacts listed in .gitignore). That can delete .env if it is ignored — check -n -x first.
On Linux you can recover a deleted untracked file only from backups or the editor; Git never had a blob.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Garbage collection
git gc --aggressive --prune=now
Packs objects, drops unreachable ones older than the prune date. Rarely needed by hand; Git runs gc in the background. After a huge filter-repo (chapter 20) you will run it on purpose.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
git fsck (peek)
git fsck --full
Reports dangling objects (often old amended commits) and real corruption. Dangling is normal. Missing blobs is chapter 21.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Hooks are Local Policy; the Server is Real Policy
A hook is an executable Git runs by filename. Exit non-zero aborts the Git operation. Client hooks are not cloned (by design: a clone must not execute a stranger’s scripts). Therefore they are courtesy. Server pre-receive / update and CI are enforcement.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

.git/hooks/pre-commit runs on this clone only, unless core.hooksPath points at a shared dir.
--no-verify skips client pre-commit and commit-msg.
The web editor on a forge never runs your laptop hooks.
core.hooksPath and init.templateDir are how a Linux user shares hooks without committing .git.

  git commit
     → pre-commit → commit-msg → object exists

  git push
     → pre-push (client) → network → pre-receive (server) → CI

title: Theory
text:
Why both
Client hooks fail in milliseconds (whitespace, WIP subject). CI fails in minutes (tests, secret scan) and cannot be skipped with --no-verify. Put the same checks in both; put policy on the server.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Forgetting chmod +x.
Hooks that print to stdout and corrupt commit-msg files.
Assuming teammates have your hooks after git clone.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Types, writing, templates vs CI, lab; then prepare-commit-msg, post-checkout/merge, --no-verify.

title: Hook Types
text:
Hook Types: Pre-Commit, Commit-Msg, Pre-Push
After this page you can name the client hooks this book uses and where they live on Linux.

title: Hook Types
section: A hook is a program Git runs
text:
A hook is a program Git runs
Executable files in .git/hooks/. Git looks at the filename. If pre-commit exists and is executable (chmod +x), Git runs it before it writes a commit object. Exit status 0 continues. Non-zero aborts.
 git commit
    │
    ▼
 pre-commit      exit ≠ 0 ──► abort, no object
    │ 0
    ▼
 commit-msg      exit ≠ 0 ──► abort, no object
    │ 0
    ▼
 commit object written, main slides forward

 git push
    │
    ▼
 pre-push        exit ≠ 0 ──► abort, remote unchanged
    │ 0
    ▼
 objects uploaded
Sample files are *.sample and are not run. Copy and chmod:
cd ~/desk/desk-api
ls .git/hooks
install -m 0755 .git/hooks/pre-commit.sample .git/hooks/pre-commit
# then edit; or write your own
install -m 0755 is the Linux way to copy and set the executable bit in one step.

title: Hook Types
text:
Client hooks you will write








Hook
When
Typical job




pre-commit
After you type git commit, before the object exists
Lint, block secrets, git diff --check


commit-msg
After you save the message
Conventional Commits pattern


pre-push
After you type git push, before objects upload
Tests, block WIP branches



There are more (prepare-commit-msg, post-commit, post-checkout). Start with these three.

title: Hook Types
text:
Server hooks (later)
A forge runs pre-receive / update / post-receive on the server when you push. Chapter 23 names them; chapter 31 uses them for policy. Your laptop hooks do not run on the server. A teammate can skip pre-commit with git commit --no-verify. Server hooks are the ones that actually enforce.

title: Hook Types
text:
Environment
Hooks run with a POSIX shell on Linux unless the shebang says otherwise. Always start with:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
Git sets GIT_DIR and runs with the working tree as cwd for client hooks (with nuances for worktrees, chapter 14). Print to stderr so you do not pollute commit output:
echo "pre-commit: running" >&2

title: Writing a Hook
text:
Writing Your First Hook
After this page you have a pre-commit that refuses a commit containing a tab-only whitespace error, and a commit-msg that checks a conventional subject.

title: Writing a Hook
text:
pre-commit
cat > ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/pre-commit <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
git diff --cached --check
EOF
chmod +x ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/pre-commit
git diff --cached --check flags leftover conflict markers and bad whitespace in the index. Exit status non-zero aborts the commit.
Try:
cd ~/desk/desk-api
printf 'bad \n' >> README.md    # trailing space
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: trigger hook"
Fix the line, git add, commit again.

title: Writing a Hook
text:
commit-msg
Git passes the path to a temporary file that holds the message:
cat > ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/commit-msg <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
file="$1"
subject="$(head -n1 "$file")"
if [[ "$subject" == WIP* ]]; then
  echo "commit-msg: subject cannot start with WIP" >&2
  exit 1
fi
EOF
chmod +x ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/commit-msg
A stricter conventional check can wait until the team agrees on types. Start by blocking WIP.

title: Writing a Hook
text:
pre-push
Git passes the remote name and URL, and on stdin: local ref, local hash, remote ref, remote hash.
cat > ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/pre-push <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
while read -r local_ref local_sha remote_ref remote_sha; do
  if [[ "$remote_ref" == refs/heads/main && "$local_sha" != "$remote_sha" ]]; then
    echo "pre-push: running tests before updating main" >&2
    # python -m pytest -q || exit 1
  fi
done
EOF
chmod +x ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/pre-push
Uncomment the test command when desk-api has tests.

title: Writing a Hook
text:
--no-verify
git commit --no-verify -m "docs: skip hooks"
Emergency only. Treat it as breaking the seatbelt.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
Hook Templates: Sharing Hooks Across Repos
After this page you can point new repos at a shared hooks directory, and you know why CI still has to run on the server.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
.git/hooks is local
Cloning does not copy hooks (Git ignores them in the payload on purpose: a clone would otherwise execute someone else’s scripts). Each clone needs its own install step.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
core.hooksPath
mkdir -p ~/desk/git-hooks
# put pre-commit, commit-msg, … there, chmod +x
git config --global core.hooksPath ~/desk/git-hooks
Every repo on this Linux user account now runs those hooks. A repo can override with git config core.hooksPath .githooks (a directory inside the project that you do commit).
Project-local, committed:
mkdir -p ~/desk/desk-api/.githooks
# copy scripts, chmod +x, commit them
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
New clones still must run the git config once, or a Makefile / just recipe / bin/install-hooks script. Document that in README.md.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
init.templateDir
mkdir -p ~/desk/git-template/hooks
# scripts in that hooks dir
git config --global init.templateDir ~/desk/git-template
git init and git clone copy the template’s hooks/ into the new .git/hooks. Good for your laptop. Teammates need the same config.

title: Hook Templates and CI
section: CI is the hook you cannot skip
text:
CI is the hook you cannot skip
A pre-commit hook is a courtesy. git commit --no-verify and a forge’s web editor skip it. CI on the forge (chapter 32, GitHub Actions in Part VI) runs on the server after push. Put the same checks there: git diff --check, tests, secret scanning.
 laptop                         forge
 .git/hooks/pre-commit          pre-receive / CI job
    │ skippable                    │ not skippable
    ▼                              ▼
 git commit                     git push accepted
    │                              │
    └──────── git push ────────────┘
Client hooks catch mistakes in milliseconds on Linux. CI is the policy. Use both.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
Frameworks
pre-commit.com is a Python manager that installs a tiny .git/hooks/pre-commit and runs a YAML list of linters. Optional. Raw bash hooks in this chapter teach the mechanism; a framework is fine in production if the team already uses it.

git restore README.md

git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: hooks lab"
git status
Clean status, new commit. Remove the hook when you are done with the lab, or leave it — --check is a good default:
rm -f .git/hooks/pre-commit
Leave it in place if you want the check on this clone.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Submodules Pin a Hash; Worktrees Share an Object Store
A submodule is a second repository whose current commit is recorded in the parent as a gitlink (mode 160000). A worktree is a second working directory for the same repository: one .git, several checkouts, one branch per worktree.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

The superproject stores a URL (.gitmodules) and a gitlink hash, not the child’s files as blobs.
git clone of the parent does not fetch submodule objects unless --recurse-submodules / submodule update --init.
Two worktrees cannot check out the same branch (indexes would fight).
Worktree .git is a file pointing at the main repo’s worktrees/ metadata.

  submodule                         worktrees

  desk-api tree                     ~/desk-api        HEAD → main
    src/desk-lib → gitlink 9fce     ~/desk-api-hf     HEAD → hotfix
  desk-lib repo  A ← 9fce                 \              /
                                           shared objects/refs

title: Theory
text:
Why not always submodule
If two projects always change together, you are paying pin-and-update tax for a monorepo’s job. If they have separate release cycles, the pin is the feature.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Committing in a submodule and forgetting to push it (parent points at a hash nobody has).
Detached HEAD in the submodule by default after update.
rm -rf a worktree directory without git worktree remove.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter

title: Submodules
text:
Submodule Mechanics: Add, Update, Clone
After this page you can attach another Git repository at a path and record which commit it should be.

title: Submodules
section: A submodule is a nested repository plus a gitlink
text:
A submodule is a nested repository plus a gitlink
desk-api might need a shared desk-lib history without merging the trees. A submodule stores a commit hash in the parent tree (a gitlink, mode 160000) and a URL in .gitmodules.
 desk-api  (superproject)
 ├── README.md
 ├── src/ping.py
 └── src/desk-lib/          gitlink 160000 → commit 9fceb02 of desk-lib
         └── (nested .git)

 desk-lib  (its own history)
 A ← B ← 9fceb02    ← the hash the parent pins
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git submodule add ~/desk/desk-lib src/desk-lib
git status
git commit -m "chore: add desk-lib submodule"
.gitmodules is a tracked file:
[submodule "src/desk-lib"]
    path = src/desk-lib
    url = /home/ada/desk/desk-lib
On Linux use an SSH URL for anything you will clone elsewhere (git@host:ada/desk-lib.git). A path only works on this machine.

title: Submodules
text:
Clone a superproject
git clone --recurse-submodules <url> desk-api
# or after a plain clone:
git submodule update --init --recursive
Without --recurse-submodules / update --init, the path exists as an empty directory.

title: Submodules
text:
Update the pin
cd src/desk-lib
git fetch
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
cd ../..
git add src/desk-lib
git commit -m "chore: bump desk-lib"
The parent records a new gitlink hash. Pulling the parent does not move the submodule until git submodule update.

title: Submodules
text:
Pitfalls

Committing in the submodule and forgetting to push it: the parent points at a hash nobody else can fetch.
Editing files in src/desk-lib while detached: git switch -c in the submodule first.
Nested submodules: --recursive on clone and update.

If the team is small and desk-lib changes with desk-api every day, a monorepo (chapter 15) or a copy may hurt less. Submodules shine when the nested project has its own release cycle.

title: Worktrees
text:
Git Worktrees: The Modern Alternative
After this page you can check out a second branch in a second directory that shares the same .git.

title: Worktrees
section: One object store, several working trees
text:
One object store, several working trees
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git worktree add ~/desk/desk-api-hotfix hotfix/timeout
Git creates ~/desk/desk-api-hotfix on a new branch hotfix/timeout (or an existing branch if you name one that is not already checked out). Both directories share objects and refs. git commit in the hotfix tree moves hotfix/timeout. main in the original tree is untouched.
 ~/desk/desk-api/                 ~/desk/desk-api-hotfix/
 working tree on main             working tree on hotfix/timeout
         \                           /
          \                         /
           └── shared .git ────────┘
               objects, refs, reflog, remotes
git worktree list

title: Worktrees
text:
Why not git clone again
A second clone duplicates objects. A worktree is cheap and sees the same remotes, stash, and reflog. You cannot check out the same branch in two worktrees; Git refuses so the two indexes cannot fight.

title: Worktrees
text:
Linux workflow
git fetch origin
git worktree add ~/desk/desk-api-pr origin/feat/ping-json
cd ~/desk/desk-api-pr
# review, run tests
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git worktree remove ~/desk/desk-api-pr
remove deletes the extra directory after the working tree is clean. git worktree prune cleans metadata if you rm -rf the directory by hand.

title: Worktrees
text:
Detached review
git worktree add --detach ~/desk/desk-api-tag v0.1.0
Inspect a tag without leaving your feature branch in the main directory.

title: Worktrees
text:
Hooks and GIT_DIR
Worktrees have .git as a file pointing at the main repo’s worktrees/… metadata. Hooks still run from core.hooksPath or the main .git/hooks. Scripts that assume .git/ is a directory should call git rev-parse --git-dir.

title: When to Use Which
text:
When to Use Which
After this page you can pick submodule, worktree, or neither for a desk problem.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Worktree
Use a worktree when one repository needs two checkouts: a hotfix while a feature is dirty, a PR review, a tag build. Same remotes, same hooks, cheap on Linux disk.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Submodule
Use a submodule when two repositories must stay separate histories, with the parent pinning a commit of the child: a shared library, a firmware blob, a docs site with its own release train.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Copy the files
If desk-lib is three Python files and only desk-api uses them, put them in desk-api. Submodule overhead is real.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Monorepo
If desk-web, desk-api, and desk-infra always change together, one repository with three directories may be simpler (chapter 15). Worktrees still apply (two branches of the monorepo). Submodules do not.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Extra clone
git clone to a second path is fine for a throwaway experiment you might delete with rm -rf. You duplicate objects until git gc. Worktree is cleaner for a second branch.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Extra remote
Two forges is remotes (chapter 11), not submodules. Push the same history twice.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Rule of thumb
Same project, two directories → worktree. Two projects, one pin → submodule. Two projects, always in lockstep → one repo.
 one repo, two checkouts     ──►  worktree
 two repos, pin a commit     ──►  submodule
 two repos, always together  ──►  one monorepo
 two forges, same history    ──►  extra remote

title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Workflow is a Policy on Names, Not a Git Feature
Git Flow, GitHub Flow, and trunk-based development are agreements about which refs are long-lived, how long a feature name lives, and how main stays deployable. Git will merge whatever you ask. The workflow is which asks you allow.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Long-lived branches diverge; every extra one is a merge or rebase tax.
Short-lived feat/* off main (GitHub Flow topology) is independent of GitHub the product.
Trunk-based requires runtime flags or very small commits so main can take unfinished code.
Monorepo vs polyrepo is a repository boundary decision; worktrees still apply; submodules usually do not in a monorepo.

 Git Flow          main + develop + release/*     high ceremony
 GitHub Flow       main + short feat/*            this book’s desk default
 Trunk-based       main + flags                   high CI, tiny commits

title: Theory
text:
Why write it down
A strategy that exists only in chat is not enforceable. Chapter 31 (governance) is how a forge requires reviews and checks. This chapter is the graph you are asking Git to keep.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Git Flow on a two-person desk-api (ceremony without versions in the wild).
Trunk-based without tests or flags.
A monorepo whose CI always builds everything.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Git Flow, GitHub Flow/trunk, flags, mono/poly, choosing; then forking, stacked changes, release tags.

title: Git Flow
text:
Git Flow: The Classic Model
After this page you can name Git Flow’s long-lived branches and when the extra machinery is worth it.

title: Git Flow
text:
The picture
main          production; tagged releases
develop       next release; features merge here
feat/…        branched from develop, merged back (often --no-ff)
release/x.y   branched from develop, hotfixes, then merge to main *and* develop
hotfix/…      branched from main, merge to main *and* develop
main is always what is in production. develop is the integration line. Features never commit straight to main.
 main     A ─────────────── H1 ── v1.2
            \             ↗
 develop     B ← C ← D ← E ← F
                  \     ↗
 feat/invoices      X ← Y

title: Git Flow
text:
Commands (shape, not a plugin)
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git switch -c develop
git switch -c feat/invoices develop
# … commits …
git switch develop
git merge --no-ff feat/invoices
git branch -d feat/invoices
--no-ff keeps a join node so git log --first-parent develop lists features.

title: Git Flow
text:
What it costs
Two long-lived branches that diverge. Every hotfix is merged twice. Release branches exist for weeks. For desk-api with one or two people, this is a lot of graph.

title: Git Flow
text:
What it buys
A support team that must ship 1.2.3 while develop already contains 2.0 work. Multiple versions in the wild. A release manager.
Use Git Flow when you actually have that. The original git-flow CLI is optional; the branch names are the model.
Chapter 31 is how a forge enforces this (protected main, required PRs). This page is the topology.

title: GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based
text:
GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based Development
After this page you can contrast a short-lived PR branch with committing to main behind flags.

title: GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based
text:
GitHub Flow (as a Git topology)
main          always deployable
feat/…        branched from main, opened as a PR, merged, deleted
There is no long-lived develop. Production is main (or a tag on it). CI on the PR is the gate.
 GitHub Flow

 main     A ← B ← C ← M          always deployable
               ↖     ↗
 feat/ping      D ← E            PR, then delete
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git switch -c feat/ping-json
# commits, push, PR, merge on the forge
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git branch -d feat/ping-json
The name “GitHub Flow” is a topology. You can do it on Forgejo or GitLab. The forge UI is a PR/MR; Git is short-lived branches off main.

title: GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based
text:
Trunk-based
Engineers commit to main (the trunk) at least daily, often several times a day. Features that are not ready stay dark behind a flag (next page). Release branches, if any, are cut from main and live days, not months.
 trunk-based

 main     A ← B ← C ← D ← E ← F     tiny commits, flags hide unfinished work
                     ╲
                      release/1.2   short-lived, if you even cut one
git switch main
# small commit
git pull --rebase
git push
Feature branches, when used, last hours. Rebase onto main before merge. --ff-only after a rebase is the usual integrate.

title: GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based
text:
Compare










Git Flow
GitHub Flow
Trunk-based




Long-lived lines
main + develop
main
main


Feature lifetime
Days–weeks
Hours–days
Hours or a flag


Release
release/* branch
Tag / deploy main

Fits

High-CI teams



desk-api in this book defaults to GitHub Flow topology: short feat/ branches, main deployable. Trunk-based is the same graph with even shorter branches.
Enforcement (required reviews, required checks) is chapter 31. The next page is flags, which make trunk-based possible.

title: Feature Flags
text:
Feature Flags and Deployment
After this page you can ship code to main that is not yet on for users.

title: Feature Flags
section: A flag is a runtime switch
text:
A flag is a runtime switch
The commit on main contains the new code. Production does not call it until a config value is true. That is how trunk-based teams merge daily without releasing half-built ping JSON.
 main     A ← B ← C ← flag-commit ← D     all on main

 production
   DESK_PING_JSON=0   →  old string path
   DESK_PING_JSON=1   →  JSON path

 Git shipped the code at flag-commit; the env var is the release.
Toy desk-api (Python, Linux):
# src/ping.py
import os

def ping():
    if os.environ.get("DESK_PING_JSON") == "1":
        return {"status": "ok"}
    return "ok"
export DESK_PING_JSON=1
python -c 'from src.ping import ping; print(ping())'
The flag lives in the environment, a file under /etc, or a later config service. Git holds the code; the flag holds the release.

title: Feature Flags
text:
What Git still does

Small commits on main (or short feat/ branches)
Revert the commit if the code is wrong (chapter 10)
The flag can stay off while you fix

A flag is not a substitute for git revert when the code crashes before the flag is read.

title: Feature Flags
text:
Cleanup
Every flag is debt. When DESK_PING_JSON is on everywhere, delete the old branch in the if and the env var. A follow-up commit: chore: remove ping JSON flag.

title: Feature Flags
text:
GitOps preview
Later parts deploy from Git. A flag in the application is still an env var on the cluster. A flag in Git (a value in desk-infra) is GitOps: changing the file and merging to main is the release. Same idea, different file.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Monorepos vs Polyrepos
After this page you can place desk-web, desk-api, and desk-infra in one Git repository or three, on purpose.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Polyrepo (this book’s default so far)
Three repositories, three histories, three remotes:
~/desk/desk-web
~/desk/desk-api
~/desk/desk-infra
Each clones, branches, and CI-runs on its own. A change that spans API and web is two pull requests. Versions of each other are documented (“web 1.2 needs api 1.4”) or ignored until something breaks.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Monorepo
One repository:
~/desk/desk/
  web/
  api/
  infra/
One git clone, one main, one PR can touch all three. CI must learn to run only what changed, or it becomes slow. Sparse checkout and partial clone (chapter 19) exist because monorepos grow.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Trade-offs









Monorepo
Polyrepo




Cross-project change
One PR
Several PRs, several versions


Access control
One repo (paths, CODEOWNERS)
Separate remotes, easier per-team ACLs


CI
Must be smart or it is slow
Simple per repo


Submodules
Rarely needed
Common for shared libs


Git scale
Packfiles, sparse, LFS
Each repo stays small

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Linux tooling
Path-based CI (git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD | grep '^api/') is how a monorepo stays fast. CODEOWNERS (chapter 31) assigns api/ to one team. None of that requires GitHub; the files are in Git.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
This book
Labs keep three polyrepos so platform chapters can push desk-api to GitLab and Forgejo independently. If your real desk is a monorepo, the Git commands are the same; only the directory layout changes. Worktrees still apply. Submodules usually do not.

title: Choosing a Strategy
text:
Choosing a Strategy
After this page you can write a short default for desk-api and know where this book will enforce it later.

title: Choosing a Strategy
section: A default for this book’s desk
text:
A default for this book’s desk

Topology: GitHub Flow — short feat/ / fix/ branches off main, delete after integrate
Integrate: rebase the feature onto main, then --ff-only or a forge squash
main: always deployable; revert to undo (never rebase published main)
Repos: polyrepo (desk-web, desk-api, desk-infra) until a chapter says otherwise
Host: Linux; hooks and CI run there first

Write it in README.md or CONTRIBUTING.md in the repo. A strategy that exists only in someone’s head is not a strategy.

title: Choosing a Strategy
text:
When to change it

Multiple supported versions in production → Git Flow release branches
Several merges to main per engineer per day and strong tests → trunk-based plus flags
One PR always touches all three desks → consider a monorepo
A compliance officer needs a merge commit per change → --no-ff on main

title: Choosing a Strategy
text:
What Git will not decide
Git will merge whatever you ask. Forges add buttons (squash, rebase, merge). Chapter 31 is branch protection, code owners, required checks. This chapter is the agreement. The next part (power skills) is internals, reflog, bisect, and repair — the tools you want when the agreement meets a bad Tuesday.

Theory: Content Addressing is the Whole Trick

commit → tree → blob
   \→ parent commit
packfile = many objects + delta chains  (disk, not mental model)

title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Single Binary is an Architectural Statement
Gitea/Forgejo keep Git hosting in one Go process, SQLite-capable. That is a complexity budget. The Forgejo fork is a governance and license theory, not a protocol fork.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

SQLite + local disk is enough until it is not (locking, size).
Actions-compatible CI is optional, not the product core. The runner is a second process.
Codeberg is Forgejo-as-a-service with community ops (chapter 29).
The Forgejo fork did not change the Git protocol. A remote is still SSH or HTTP.

one binary ──► git repos on disk
            ──► SQLite/Postgres
            ──► optional runners

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Expecting GitLab-class HA from a hobby compose file.
Treating a current Gitea database as a drop-in for current Forgejo. The hard fork ended that promise.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter

title: Origins and Philosophy
text:
Origins and Philosophy
After this page you can say what problem a single-binary forge is built to solve, and which project solved it first.

title: Origins and Philosophy
text:
Two forks, one shape
Gogs was a lightweight Git server in Go. Development sat behind one maintainer. In 2016 contributors forked it and called the result Gitea: the same idea, with a group that could review and release.
The idea is small on purpose.
one Go process
  ├── Git repositories as bare repos on disk
  ├── issues, pull requests, users  →  one database
  └── HTTP on port 3000, and SSH for the Git remote
Default database is SQLite, a file next to the repositories. Postgres and MySQL are configuration, not a requirement. There is no separate Rails app, no Gitaly, no search cluster. Chapter 23 named those boxes. This product leaves most of them empty until you opt in.

title: Origins and Philosophy
section: What you get on the first afternoon
text:
What you get on the first afternoon
A Gitea or Forgejo instance gives a small team:

repositories, with SSH and HTTP remotes (chapter 11)
issues and pull requests
a web UI to browse files and diffs
organizations, teams, and repository permissions
webhooks, when you want an outside CI to notice a push (chapter 32)

Packages, Actions, and a container registry exist. They are extra processes and extra disks. The core stays the binary plus the data directory.

title: Origins and Philosophy
section: What this shape refuses to be
text:
What this shape refuses to be
GitLab’s theory is one application for the whole lifecycle (chapter 24): Git, CI, registry, and security scanning in one product. Gitea’s theory is the opposite budget. A desk, a lab, or a small company can run it on a machine that would struggle to boot GitLab Omnibus.
That budget is the point. The moment the database, the Git files, and CI runners all need to scale independently, you have left the afternoon install and entered chapter 36. The binary does not stop you. It also does not hide the work.
The next page is why Forgejo exists as a second project with this same shape.

title: The Forgejo Fork
text:
The Forgejo Fork
After this page you can explain why Forgejo split from Gitea, and what that split changes for an operator.

title: The Forgejo Fork
text:
Who holds the name
Gitea’s code was community-run. In 2022 a for-profit company, Gitea Ltd, took the trademark and the project’s direction. An open letter from contributors went unanswered. In October 2022 Codeberg and other operators published Forgejo as a fork.
Codeberg e.V., a non-profit in Berlin, holds the Forgejo domains. Forgejo has not registered a trademark. The public forge at codeberg.org runs Forgejo. Chapter 29 is that hosted instance. This chapter is the software you run yourself.
Gogs (single maintainer)
  └── Gitea, 2016          Gitea Ltd, MIT, company edition
        └── Forgejo, Oct 2022
              soft fork through 2023
              hard fork, early 2024     Codeberg e.V., GPL-3.0-or-later since v9

title: The Forgejo Fork
text:
Soft fork, then hard fork
Through 2023 Forgejo was a soft fork: it tracked Gitea and stayed a drop-in. Changing the download URL was enough to upgrade a Gitea server onto Forgejo.
On 15 February 2024 the project became a hard fork. Stable Forgejo stopped promising to contain all of Gitea. The codebases diverge on purpose, so each side can change without rebasing onto the other. A Gitea database from the 1.22 era is the last generation where people treated the switch as a binary swap. Later pairs need the Forgejo upgrade guide for those two versions. Do not point a new Forgejo binary at a production Gitea data directory and hope.

title: The Forgejo Fork
text:
What actually changed
The Git protocol did not change. Clients, remotes, and hooks from Parts I–III work against either UI.
What changed is governance and the license:

GPL-3.0-or-later means a modified Forgejo you ship to others comes with source under the same terms. MIT does not require that. Gitea can legally ship a closed Enterprise build on the same code. Forgejo’s license is how the project refuses that path.
Day to day, issues, pull requests, and the settings screens still feel like the same product. Actions exist on both (Forgejo Actions and Gitea Actions), with a runner you install separately. Federation between Forgejo instances is a Forgejo project and is not something to design a company on until you have tried it on the version you run.
The next page puts Forgejo, Gitea, and GitLab in one table. The lab pins Forgejo 15 LTS, not whatever tag your registry calls latest.
